'''Solid oxide fuel cell''' is a common [[fuel cell]] design known for

* efficiency
* high operating temperature
** relatively long startup time
** need for integrated heat management system

<ref>{{#cite:Q4257}}</ref>

== Operation<ref>{{#cite:Q4257}}</ref> ==

[[File:SOFC-schema.png|thumbnail|Simplified SOFC operation schema]]
=== Cathode ===

[[File:SOFC-1.mp4|thumbnail|SOFC cathode operation schema]]
$$
\frac{1}{2}O_2+2e^- \to O^{2-}
$$

=== Ionic diffusion through electrolyte ===

[[File:SOFC-2.mp4|thumbnail|SOFC ionic diffusion operation schema]]
[[File:SOFC-3.mp4|thumbnail|SOFC ionic diffusion operation schema 2]]
The most common electrolyte in a SOFC is doped $ZrO_2$ ionised by heating to $600-1000^\circ C$. The dopent cations ($Ca,Mg,Y$, 2+ or 3+, compared to 4+ for $Zr^{4+}$) creates vacancies allowing for the transport of $O^{2-}$.

=== Anode (fuel combustion) ===

Various [[fuel]]s can be used at the anode of an SOFC:

* $H_2,CO$ ('''most common''')

$$
CO+O^{2-} \to CO_2+ 2e^-
H_2+O^{2-} \to H_2O + 2e^-
$$

* Hydrocarbons: diesel, gasoline, alcohol, natural gas, etc.

== Limitations ==

The high operation temperature of SOFCs make it less suitable for mobile/intermittent applications. As a result, SOFCs are most commonly used in electricity generators as of now, although recent advancements in [[supercapacitor batteries]], which can be used to shorten the startup time of SOFCs, are opening up the way to new applications such as in heavy passenger/goods vehicles.
